passages.happening:
“Now there was another famine in the land, subsequent to the one that had occurred in Abraham’s time” (verse 1). Isaac goes to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar.

The LORD appears to him. “Do not go down to Egypt. Settle in the land where I tell you” (verse 2). “Stay in this land as a foreigner, and I will be with you and bless you” (verse 3).

God repeats to Isaac what he promised Abraham: the land, descendants “as numerous as the stars in the sky”, and blessing for “all nations of the earth” (verse 4). He gives a reason: “because Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws” (verse 5).

“So Isaac settled in Gerar” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
This is the one chapter in Genesis where Isaac stands at the center. Almost everything in it echoes his father's life: a famine, a stay in Gerar, a wife called a sister, quarrels over wells, an oath with Abimelech, and the naming of Beersheba. Isaac walks in his father's footsteps, in faith and in failure.

In Canaan the harvest depended on rain. When the rain failed, people went to Egypt, where the Nile flooded every year and the fields still grew. Abraham went there in a famine (12:10). Isaac is told not to go. He never leaves the land of promise in his whole life.

‘Stay as a foreigner’ translates a Hebrew word for living as a guest in someone else's land, without owning it. That was Isaac's life, as it had been Abraham's.

‘I will be with you’ is the first time God speaks to Isaac in Genesis. It is the heart of the promise. Before land or children, God promises himself.

Gerar lay in the dry south, between Gaza and Beersheba. The note on Genesis 20 explains that ‘Abimelech’ may have been a royal title, used by more than one ruler. The king here may be the same man as in Abraham's day, now old, or a later king with the same name. The text does not say.

‘The land of the Philistines’ raises the same puzzle as in chapter 21. The Philistines known from archaeology settled on the southern coast in the 1100s BC, long after the time usually given for Abraham. Some think the writer used a later, familiar name for the region. Some think earlier groups from the Aegean Sea were already there. Some think the stories took their final shape in a later time. These notes do not settle it.
passages.later:
Hebrews says Abraham lived in the land “as a stranger in a foreign country. He lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise” (Hebrews 11:9).

Paul reads the promise of blessing for the nations as good news told ahead of time, and says it comes through faith (Galatians 3:8). He adds that the law came 430 years later and “does not revoke the covenant previously established by God” (Galatians 3:17).

James looks at Abraham's obedience and says “his faith was working with his actions” (James 2:22).

God will say the same words, ‘I am with you’, to Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:15), and Jesus says them to his disciples at the end of Matthew's Gospel (Matthew 28:20).
passages.hard:
How could Abraham keep God's ‘statutes’ and ‘laws’ long before the law was given to Moses at Mount Sinai? Verse 5 uses the full set of words later used for that law.

Readers explain it in more than one way. Many read the words broadly. Abraham did what God told him: he left his home, he was circumcised, he took Isaac to Moriah. The writer uses the words his readers knew for obeying God. Later Jewish tradition took the verse more literally. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, cites this verse to say that Abraham kept the whole law before it was given (Kiddushin 4:14). Many critical scholars think the wording comes from a later editor shaped by the language of Deuteronomy.

A second question follows. Did Abraham earn the blessing? In chapter 15 God made his promise as a free gift, and Abraham believed it. Here the promise is confirmed ‘because Abraham listened’. Most Christian readers hold both together. The promise rests on God's grace. Abraham's obedience was the fruit of his trust, not the price of the promise.
passages.asks: God told Isaac to stay where he was, in a hard year, and promised to be with him there. Ask where you are tempted to run to what looks safer. Then ask what it would mean to trust that God is with you in the place you are.

passages.t: ‘She is my sister’, a third time
passages.happening:
The men of Gerar ask about Rebekah. Isaac says, “She is my sister.” He is afraid that “The men of this place will kill me on account of Rebekah, because she is so beautiful” (verse 7).

After a long time, Abimelech looks down from a window and sees “Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah” (verse 8).

He sends for Isaac. “So she is really your wife! How could you say, ‘She is my sister’?” Isaac answers, “Because I thought I might die on account of her” (verse 9).

“What is this you have done to us?” Abimelech asks. “One of the people could easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us” (verse 10). Then he warns everyone: “Whoever harms this man or his wife will surely be put to death” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This is the third time in Genesis that a husband passes off his wife as his sister. Abraham did it in Egypt (chapter 12) and in this same town of Gerar (chapter 20). The note on Genesis 20 explains the two main ways readers take the three stories: as versions of one old story placed side by side, or as a family failing in the same way again and again. On either view, the promise is put at risk by the man who carries it, and God keeps it safe.

Isaac's lie is weaker than his father's. Sarah really was Abraham's half-sister. Rebekah was a relative from his father's family, the granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor (24:15), not his sister. There is no half-truth to hide behind.

The word for ‘caressing’ is a play on Isaac's name. Isaac means ‘he laughs’, and the same Hebrew root can mean to laugh, to play or to caress. The king sees Isaac ‘Isaac-ing’ with his wife. Tenderness gives the lie away.

Once again the outsider has the working conscience. Abimelech speaks of guilt, as the king in chapter 20 did. He protects Isaac and Rebekah with his own law. The man of the promise was afraid of strangers, and the stranger turned out to be just.

This time no one takes Rebekah. The danger is caught before it happens. But Isaac had left his wife open to it, to protect himself.
passages.later:
The note on Genesis 20 points to the same pattern in Abraham, and to the psalm that looks back on these years: “He rebuked kings on their behalf” (Psalm 105:14).

The Bible often shows fear passing down a family. Exodus speaks of the guilt of fathers reaching the children (Exodus 34:7). And Ezekiel adds the other side: a son does not have to repeat his father's sins (Ezekiel 18:14-17).

Peter tells husbands to “treat your wives with consideration as a delicate vessel, and with honor” (1 Peter 3:7). Isaac did the opposite. He protected himself and put his wife in harm's way.
passages.hard: A word of care. Some readers have been put at risk by someone who should have protected them: a husband, a wife, a parent. This story does not call that right, and neither does Abimelech. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are in danger now, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Isaac repeated his father's failure, almost word for word. Ask what fear you learned at home and still carry. Then ask whom it puts at risk, and what it would look like to trust God instead of the old habit.

passages.happening:
“Now Isaac sowed seed in the land, and that very year he reaped a hundredfold. And the LORD blessed him” (verse 12). He becomes very rich, with flocks, herds and servants, “that the Philistines envied him” (verse 14).

The Philistines fill in all the wells that Abraham's servants had dug (verse 15). Abimelech tells Isaac, “Depart from us, for you are much too powerful for us” (verse 16).

Isaac moves to the Valley of Gerar. He reopens his father's wells and gives them “the same names his father had given them” (verse 18).

His servants dig a new well, and the herdsmen of Gerar say, “The water is ours!” Isaac names it Esek (verse 20). They quarrel over another, and he names it Sitnah (verse 21). He moves on and digs again, and this time no one quarrels. He names it Rehoboth and says, “At last the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Isaac was a herder, but here he plants a crop too. Herders in that land often sowed fields where the rain allowed. A hundredfold harvest, a hundred times what was sown, would be astonishing in the dry south. The writer gives the reason plainly: the LORD blessed him.

In the dry south, a well meant life. It also showed a claim to the land around it. To fill in a man's wells with dirt was an act of war without weapons, a way to drive him off. To reopen them and give them back their old names was to say, ‘My father dug these, and I am his son.’

The names of the new wells tell the story. Esek means ‘quarrel’ or ‘contention’. Sitnah means ‘opposition’ or ‘hostility’. Rehoboth means ‘broad places’ or ‘room’.

Notice what Isaac does not do. He does not fight. Each time the herdsmen claim a well, he moves on and digs another. He gives way, again and again, until there is room. Some readers call this weakness. Others see a man who trusted God to make space for him, and found that God did.

Blessing brings envy. Isaac did nothing wrong by growing rich, but his neighbors felt threatened. The text does not blame Isaac or praise the Philistines. It shows how often God's gifts stir up trouble with others.
passages.later:
Jesus' parable of the sower speaks of seed that fell on good soil and produced a crop “a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold” (Matthew 13:8).

The word behind Rehoboth, ‘to make room’, is used in the Psalms for God setting a person free from distress: “You have relieved my distress” (Psalm 4:1).

Jesus said, “Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5), and Paul wrote, “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone” (Romans 12:18). Isaac at the wells is one picture of what that can look like.
passages.asks: Isaac moved on from a fight he could have had, and God made room for him. Ask where you are digging the same well over and over, sure it is yours. Then ask whether God may be making room somewhere else, if you would let go.

passages.t: ‘I am with you’ at Beersheba, and an oath
passages.happening:
Isaac goes up to Beersheba. That night the LORD appears to him: “I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of My servant Abraham” (verse 24). Isaac builds an altar, calls on the name of the LORD, and pitches his tent there (verse 25).

Abimelech comes from Gerar with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol his army commander. “Why have you come to me?” Isaac asks. “You hated me and sent me away” (verse 27).

They answer, “We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you” (verse 28). They ask for an oath and a covenant that Isaac will not harm them (verse 29).

Isaac makes them a feast (verse 30). Early the next morning they swear an oath, and he sends them away in peace (verse 31). That same day his servants tell him, “We have found water!” He names the well Shibah, “and to this day the name of the city is Beersheba” (verses 32-33).
passages.hearers:
God's words at Beersheba begin with ‘Do not be afraid’. Isaac had been afraid in Gerar, afraid enough to lie. Now God speaks to the fear itself. The answer to fear is not a plan. It is a presence: ‘I am with you’.

The chapter is framed by two visits from the LORD, at the start (verses 2-5) and here. Each one promises the same thing, God's presence.

Isaac builds an altar, as Abraham did. Then he pitches his tent and his servants dig a well. Worship comes first, then home, then water. Many readers notice the order.

The same king who sent Isaac away now comes asking for peace. He brings his chief soldier. A powerful local ruler wants a sworn agreement with a newcomer whose success has made him dangerous. Abraham made the same kind of agreement in chapter 21.

Isaac could have refused. Instead he gives them a meal. In that world a shared meal sealed an agreement. The oath the next morning made it binding.

Beersheba means ‘well of the oath’ or ‘well of seven’. In Hebrew the words for ‘oath’ and ‘seven’ sound alike. Shibah is close to both. Genesis tells how the name came about in Abraham's day (21:31) and again here. Some readers take it as two stories about one place, others as a son renewing his father's claim. Either way the well and the oath belong together.
passages.later:
Isaac's peace with his enemies fits Jesus' words: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). And Proverbs says that when a man's ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him (Proverbs 16:7).

Beersheba became the southern edge of Israel's land. ‘From Dan to Beersheba’ meant the whole country (Judges 20:1).

God names himself again as ‘the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob’ when he calls Moses (Exodus 3:6). Jesus quotes it to show that God is the God of the living (Matthew 22:32).
passages.asks: God said ‘Do not be afraid’ to a man who had just been ruled by fear. Ask what you are afraid of right now. Then ask whether there is someone who once wronged you with whom you could share a meal and make peace, as Isaac did.

passages.happening:
“When Esau was forty years old, he took as his wives Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite” (verse 34).

“And they brought grief to Isaac and Rebekah” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Esau marries at forty, the same age as his father (25:20). But he marries two women at once, and both are from the local peoples of Canaan.

Abraham had made his servant swear not to take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites (24:3). He wanted a wife from his own family, who would share the faith of the house. Esau goes the other way and does not ask.

Who these Hittites were is not certain. The best-known Hittites ruled an empire far to the north, in what is now Turkey. Many scholars think the Hittites of Canaan, whom chapter 23 meets at Hebron, were a local people with a similar name.

‘Grief’ here is strong. The Hebrew speaks of bitterness of spirit. The text does not say what the wives did. It says only that the marriages brought sorrow to both parents.

These two verses are a bridge. They prepare for the next chapter's family crisis and for Rebekah's complaint at its end (27:46). They also show a family already divided. Esau, the father's favorite, is going his own way.
passages.later:
Rebekah will say, “I am weary of my life because of these Hittite women” (Genesis 27:46). Esau later tries to please his father by marrying a daughter of Ishmael (Genesis 28:8-9).

Israel's law later warns against marriages that would turn God's people to other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). Paul gives Christians a similar warning (2 Corinthians 6:14).

Hebrews remembers Esau as one who treated holy things lightly (Hebrews 12:16).
passages.asks: Esau's choices brought grief to his parents, and the text does not tell us all his reasons. Ask whether a grown child's choices, or your own, have opened a wound in your family. Then ask what it would look like to keep loving across that wound, as the story will show is possible.
